edbDesc: Luminescence produced in a material by the bombardment of ionizing radiation such as beta particles. Examples include the tritium-excited luminous paints used on watch dials and gun sights.
title: Radioluminescence
description: Some materials glow when struck by radiation from radioactive substances, each particle making a tiny flash of light. In 1903 William Crookes looked through a lens at a zinc sulfide screen near a speck of radium, saw it sparkle with countless separate flashes, and built the spinthariscope to show it. Tritium-lit watch hands and exit signs, and the scintillation counters that detect radiation, use it.
effect: radiation hitting certain materials makes them flash or glow with light
usedIn: Tritium-lit watch hands, gun sights and exit signs
Scintillation counters and hospital gamma cameras
Detectors in PET and CT scanners
strength: Each alpha particle makes a flash just visible to dark-adapted eyes; a tritium exit sign glows with no power for 10-20 years, but only bright enough to see in the dark.
pickWhy: Canonical card for radiation-made light (Scintillation merges here); broadest common name. Crookes's deck cards are different works.
